newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces fight for Bagram airbase.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces fight for Bagram airbase.

text.p: Afghan opposition forces have advanced to within a few km (miles) of the Bagram military airbase north of Kabul held by the Islamic Taleban militia, military and opposition sources said on Saturday.

A military source who asked not to be named said guerrillas loyal to former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood had launched an offensive on Thursday, driving the Taleban out of the town of Jabal-os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul.
They were were now fighting for the Soviet-built Bagram airbase, 50 km (31 miles) from the capital.
The source said the Taleban had repulsed an assault on Bagram on Friday, but some fighting was continuing. He had no immediate word on casualties on either side.
He said Masood's forces had advanced southwards along the road from Jabal-os-Siraj and were fighting for control of a damaged bridge at Pul-i-Matak, north of the town of Charikar.
Dr Abdullah, a close aide to Masood, told Reuters by satellite telephone that fighting around Bagram had subsided on Saturday, but artillery fire was continuing near Jabal-os-Siraj.
Masood captured Jabal-os-Siraj about two weeks ago, cutting off a Taleban force that had crossed the Salang Pass through the Hind Kush mountains into opposition-held northern Afghanistan.
The Taleban were unable to reopen the pass to resupply their comrades, who were driven from their last foothold in the north when the town of Pul-i-Khumri fell to their foes on Wednesday.

The Taleban, bent on imposing strict Islamic rule throughout Afghanistan, have suffered a series of defeats since their fighters entered the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif last month after an opposition commander briefly changed sides.
The mainly ethnic Uzbek troops of the commander, General Abdul Malik, turned on the Taleban and with the help of the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat militia drove them from the city.

The anti-Taleban alliance, which includes Malik's Junbish-i-Milli faction, the Jamiat-i-Islami party led by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani, and Hezb-i-Wahdat agreed on Thursday to set up a new provisional government.
Rabbani, whose government was forced out of Kabul by the Taleban in September, had talks with Malik on Saturday.

The meeting, held in Mazar-i-Sharif, covered relations between the Rabbani government and the wider anti-Taleban alliance, formally known as the United National and Islamic Front for the Salvation of Afghanistan.

"After recent events, questions had arisen about the nature of the linkages between the United Front and the (Rabbani-led government of the) Islamic State of Afghanistan," Rabbani told reporters after the talks.
Malik, still allied with the Taleban at the time, became head of Junbish-i-Milli two weeks ago after forcing its previous leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, to flee to Turkey.
"The United Front and Junbish-i-Milli under General Malik decisively support the Islamic State of Afghanistan," said Rabbani.
On Friday the United Front announced plans to form a new government dominated by people not linked to the factions that fought the Soviet-backed communist government in the 1980s.
"After this exchange of views we are hoping to reach a decision about the composition of a new broad-based government," Rabbani said, but stressed there would be no change at the top.
"There is a need for some changes in the government, but the leadership of the Islamic State will remain the same," he said.
"In the past one of the government's main problems was the insistence of the parties to have shares in the cabinet.

"Not all those selected were in a position to perform their duty...The parties of the United Front have agreed to nominate specialists and technocrats for positions in the new government," Rabbani said.
